facts.statement: Europejara lived in Spain during the Barremian age of the Early Cretaceous, 125 to 121 million years ago.
facts.quote: Europejara is a genus of tapejarid pterosaur, a flying reptile that lived in what is now Spain during the Barremian age of the Early Cretaceous epoch, 125 to 121 million years ago.

facts.statement: The genus and species Europejara olcadesorum were named in 2012.
facts.quote: In 2012, the new genus and species Europejara olcadesorum was named based on it.

facts.statement: The holotype consists of an incomplete, crushed skull with displaced postorbital bones and an almost complete mandible.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen consists of an incomplete, crushed skull; the bones of the postorbital region are displaced while the mandible is almost complete.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest it was frugivorous or granivorous and played a role in seed dispersal when angiosperms first appeared.
facts.quote: Due to the shape of their skulls and jaws, they have been considered frugivorous (fruit-eaters) and/or granivorous (seed-eaters), and the age of Europejara led its describers to suggest that tapejarids had a role in seed dispersal when angiosperms (flowering plants) first appeared.

facts.statement: It lived in a subtropical wetland environment represented by the La Huérguina Formation.
facts.quote: Europejara is known from the La Huérguina Formation, which represents a subtropical wetland environment.

facts.statement: The locality belongs to the La Huérguina Formation and dates to the late Barremian of the Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: The locality belongs to the La Huérguina Formation and dates to the late Barremian of the Early Cretaceous.

facts.statement: The site was discovered in 1985 and yielded over 20,000 fossils by 2023.
facts.quote: The site was discovered in 1985, and as of 2023, nearly 30 excavation campaigns have yielded over 20,000 fossils

facts.statement: Romain Vullo and colleagues reported a new pterosaur skull from Las Hoyas in 2012.
facts.quote: In 2012, the palaeontologist Romain Vullo and colleagues reported an incomplete skull of a pterosaur (an extinct order of flying reptiles) from Las Hoyas, new to science.

facts.statement: The specimen designated MCCM-LH 9413 was made the holotype of Europejara olcadesorum.
facts.quote: The specimen (designated as MCCM-LH 9413 in the Las Hoyas collection of the Museo de las Ciencias de Castilla–La Mancha) was made the holotype of the new genus and species Europejara olcadesorum.

facts.statement: The specimen includes scattered plates forming the scleral ring and two elements of the hyoid bone.
facts.quote: Several scattered plates that formed the scleral ring (a bony ring inside the eye) and two elements of the hyoid (tongue bone) are also present.

facts.statement: No soft tissue or keratinous parts are preserved.
facts.quote: No integument, such as soft tissue and keratinous parts, is preserved.

facts.statement: In 2012, researchers estimated the wingspan of the small pterosaur Europejara to be around 2 meters.
facts.quote: Based on the proportions of other tapejarids, the describers of Europejara considered it a relatively small pterosaur in 2012, with an estimated wingspan of around 2 m.

facts.statement: In 2023, the same researchers revised the estimated wingspan of Europejara to between 3 and 4 meters, classifying it as a mid-sized pterosaur.
facts.quote: In 2023, some of the same authors gave a wingspan of 3 - 4 m, considering Europejara a mid-sized pterosaur.

facts.statement: Europejara, a member of the tapejarid family, is characterized by having a short face and downturned jaw tips.
facts.quote: Tapejarids are characterised by their short faces and downturned jaw tips.

facts.statement: The fossil record of Europejara consists only of skull bones.
facts.quote: Europejara is only known from skull bones

facts.statement: Europejara was covered in hair-like pycnofibres and possessed extensive wing membranes.
facts.quote: As a pterosaur, Europejara was covered with hair-like pycnofibres and had extensive wing membranes

facts.statement: The lower temporal fenestra at the back of the Europejara skull was narrow.
facts.quote: The lower temporal fenestra (the opening behind the orbit) at the back of the skull of Europejara was narrow

facts.statement: Europejara possessed a deep, bony crest projecting downward from the dentaries that was recurved backwards and more developed vertically than horizontally.
facts.quote: Europejara had a deep, bony crest that projected downward from the dentaries and was distinct from those of its relatives in being recurved backwards and more developed from top to bottom than from front to back.

facts.statement: The dentary crest of Europejara was at least 90 mm deep, which is four times deeper than the back of its lower jaw.
facts.quote: The crest was at least 90 mm deep, four times deeper than the back of the lower jaw

facts.statement: In 2012, Vullo and colleagues classified Europejara as a member of the pterosaur family Tapejaridae.
facts.quote: Europejara was classified as a member of the pterosaur family Tapejaridae by Vullo and colleagues in the phylogenetic analysis accompanying their 2012 description.

facts.statement: In 2016, Rubi Vargas Pêgas and colleagues identified Europejara as the sister group to the Brazilian genera Caiuajara, Tapejara, and Tupandactylus.
facts.quote: In their 2016 description of the tapejarid Aymberedactylus, the palaeontologist Rubi Vargas Pêgas and colleagues found Europejara to be the sister group of the Brazilian genera Caiuajara, Tapejara, and Tupandactylus.

facts.statement: In 2019, Alexander W. Kellner and colleagues named the tribe Tapejarini to include Europejara and its Brazilian relatives.
facts.quote: The palaeontologist Alexander W. Kellner (one of the describers of Europejara) and colleagues named the tribe Tapejarini for the clade containing Europejara and its Brazilian relatives in their 2019 description of Keresdrakon.

facts.statement: Europejara lived during the Barremian age in Spain, indicating that tapejarids were distributed across Gondwana and Laurasia earlier than previously known.
facts.quote: The describers stated that the presence of a tapejarid in Spain during the Barremian age shows that the group was distributed earlier and more broadly throughout the palaeocontinents of Gondwana (the southern continent) and Laurasia (the northern continent) than previously known, living from Brazil to China.

facts.statement: It is debated whether tapejarids originated in Laurasia or Gondwana, with some researchers arguing that the monophyly of Chinese tapejarines does not support a Laurasian origin.
facts.quote: These researchers noted that, since Chinese tapejarines form a monophyletic (natural) clade rather than a paraphyletic (unnatural) group, this does not support a Laurasian origin over a Gondwanan one

facts.statement: More research is needed to support interpretations regarding the dispersal patterns and origins of tapejarids, including the relationship of Europejara to South American taxa.
facts.quote: the authors noted more work was needed to support these interpretations.

facts.statement: In 2012, researchers Vullo and colleagues identified a unique dentary crest shape in Europejara not seen in other pterosaurs.
facts.quote: Writing in 2012, Vullo and colleagues found the shape of Europejaras dentary crest to be unlike any previously described among pterosaurs.

facts.statement: In 2013, Mark Witton described tapejarids as adaptable, generalist fliers comparable to modern parrots and crows.
facts.quote: The palaeontologist Mark Witton summarised ideas of tapejarid locomotor abilities in 2013, stating that tapejarids were adaptable, generalist fliers, similar to extant parrots and crows.

facts.statement: Tapejarids likely flew in inland areas due to their short wings, while their long, well-muscled limbs aided in launching and flapping.
facts.quote: Their relatively short wings appear consistent with flying in inland areas, and their long limbs and probably well-muscled limb girdles would have made them adept at launching and flapping.

facts.statement: Tapejarids are thought to have been frugivorous or granivorous based on their short skulls, shaped jaws, and lack of teeth.
facts.quote: Tapejarids are thought to have been good fliers with excellent vision and have mainly been considered frugivorous (fruit-eaters) and/or granivorous (seed-eaters), based on their short skulls, downturned and unusually shaped jaws, and their lack of teeth.

facts.statement: Tapejarid beaks were likely covered by a rhamphotheca, with some possibly having pointed projections similar to omnivorous birds like toucans.
facts.quote: The beak was probably covered by a rhamphotheca (a keratinous covering), and while shaped like the underlying bone as in modern birds, the bills of some tapejarids might have had pointed projections as in omnivorous birds such as toucans.

facts.statement: Researchers suggested tapejarids might have had a herbivorous or omnivorous diet including seeds, fruits, insects, and small vertebrates, though this lacks direct fossil evidence.
facts.quote: While conceding this comparison lacks fossil evidence, these researchers suggested tapejarids could also have had a herbivorous or omnivorous diet that included seeds, fruits, insects, and small vertebrate animals.

facts.statement: Phytoliths in Sinopterus included those from grasses, gymnosperms, and ferns, indicating a diverse plant diet.
facts.quote: Some of the phytoliths were identified as belonging to the angiosperm family Poaceae (grasses), as well as to gymnosperms or ferns, indicating that Sinopterus had a diverse plant diet.

facts.statement: Bite-force estimations and skull similarities between Tapejara and Sinopterus support a herbivorous diet of fruits, seeds, and resistant plant matter for both.
facts.quote: They stated that bite-force estimations of Tapejara had suggested a herbivorous diet of fruits, seeds, and more resistant plant matter, and added that the similarity between the skulls of Tapejara and Sinopterus indicated similar bite forces, supporting a herbivorous diet for both.

facts.statement: Europejara was recovered from the Las Hoyas site in the La Huérguina Formation, dated to the late Barremian of the Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: The Las Hoyas site in the La Huérguina Formation, from which Europejara was recovered, has been dated to the late Barremian of the Early Cretaceous.

facts.statement: The Late Barremian was previously dated to 129.4–126.3 million years ago, though boundary dates have since been revised.
facts.quote: The Late Barremian has been previously dated to about 129.4–126.3 million years ago, but the age of the Barremian boundaries has since been changed to different values.

facts.statement: The Las Hoyas deposits represent a continental, subtropical wetland environment situated between a lake and a tree fern-dominated savannah over low-relief karst terrain.
facts.quote: These deposits represent a continental, subtropical wetland environment, between a lacustrine environment and a tree fern-dominated savannah, which overlaid a low-relief karstic terrain.

facts.statement: The terrestrial flora at Las Hoyas was dominated by Cheirolepidiaceae conifers, Matoniacea and Schizaeaceae ferns, and diverse angiosperms.
facts.quote: The terrestrial macroflora of Las Hoyas is dominated by conifers of the family Cheirolepidiaceae and ferns of the families Matoniacea and Schizaeaceae, as well as relatively diverse angiosperms.

facts.statement: The Las Hoyas biota consisted mainly of aquatic organisms, with rare terrestrial forms and exceptional large forms like dinosaurs.
facts.quote: The biota of Las Hoyas consists mainly of aquatic organisms, with amphibious forms less abundant, terrestrial forms rare, and large forms (such as dinosaurs) exceptional.

facts.statement: Pterosaurs were rare at Las Hoyas, with Europejara, a large anhanguerid, and a small istiodactylid represented in the fossil record.
facts.quote: Pterosaurs are rare; in addition to Europejara, a few teeth indicate the presence of a large anhanguerid and a small istiodactylid.

facts.statement: The eutriconodont mammal Spinolestes, known from a specimen preserving internal organs, was found at Las Hoyas.
facts.quote: The eutriconodont mammal Spinolestes, a specimen of which preserves internal organs, is from Las Hoyas.

facts.statement: Researchers cautioned that more fossils and gut-content analysis are needed to determine if tapejarids co-evolved with angiosperms or merely dispersed them incidentally.
facts.quote: They cautioned that more research was required to establish whether the two groups co-evolved or if tapejarids were incidental vectors, with more fossils and gut-content needed for confirmation.
